content: MT-TH, also known as mitochondrially encoded tRNA histidine, is a transfer RNA molecule encoded by the mitochondrial MT-TH gene in humans. The MT-TH gene is located on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 69 base pairs. Structurally, tRNA molecules exhibit a distinctive folded shape, characterized by three hairpin loops, resembling a three-leafed clover. MT-TH is a small transfer RNA consisting of 69 nucleotides (mapped to human mitochondrial DNA positions 12138–12206). Its primary function is to transfer the amino acid histidine to a growing polypeptide chain at the ribosomal site during protein synthesis, a process known as translation. Mutations in the MT-TH gene can lead to multiple mitochondrial deficiencies and associated disorders. These include mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), cardiomyopathy, and the MELAS/MERRF overlap syndrome. Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like Episodes (MELAS) A small number of individuals with symptoms of MELAS have been found to harbor mutations in the MT-TH gene. MELAS is a rare mitochondrial disorder that affects multiple organ systems, particularly the nervous system and brain. Symptoms of MELAS include recurrent severe headaches, muscle weakness (myopathy), hearing loss, stroke-like episodes with loss of consciousness, seizures, and other neurological complications. MELAS/MERRF Overlap Syndrome MELAS syndrome can co-occur with another mitochondrial disorder called myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF syndrome). In addition to the symptoms of MELAS, individuals with this overlap syndrome may experience muscle twitches (myoclonus), difficulty coordinating movements (ataxia), and abnormal muscle cells known as ragged-red fibers. This combination of symptoms is referred to as the MELAS/MERRF overlap syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the MT-TH gene. The exact mechanism by which these mutations disrupt mitochondrial energy production and lead to the symptoms of these syndromes remains unclear. A specific mutation, 12147G>A in the MT-TH gene, has been identified as a cause of the MELAS/MERRF overlap syndrome. A patient with this mutation exhibited symptoms such as migrainous headaches, vomiting, left hemiparesis, lateral homonymous hemianopia, and other features consistent with the overlap syndrome. The patient initially presented with symptoms of MELAS, which later progressed into the overlap syndrome. Cardiomyopathy Mutations in the MT-TH gene can also result in cardiomyopathy, a condition characterized by thickening of the heart muscle, particularly in the interventricular septum. This thickening weakens the heart muscle, impairing its ability to pump blood effectively. Patients with MT-TH mutations have been observed to develop cardiomyopathy without other common signs of mitochondrial disease, such as neurological abnormalities. The reason why these mutations specifically cause isolated cardiomyopathy remains unclear. A specific mutation, 12192G>A in the MT-TH gene, has been identified in multiple patients with cardiomyopathy, who exhibited varying forms of the condition. Deafness, Nonsyndromic Sensorineural, Mitochondrial Mutations in the MT-TH gene have also been associated with nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness. Heteroplasmic 12201T>C transitions in the MT-TH gene have been identified in a family with symptoms of nonsyndromic sensorineural hearing loss. The onset and severity of hearing loss varied among affected family members.
